beats.text: Two hundred patients come into a clinic. One hundred really have the disease. One hundred are healthy.
An AI model checks each of them, and says one of two things: alarm, or no alarm.
Of the hundred sick patients, the model raises the alarm for ninety. Those are true positives.
It misses ten. They are sick, but the model stayed quiet. False negatives. These are the dangerous ones.
Of the hundred healthy patients, ninety-five get no alarm. True negatives.
And five get an alarm they did not need. False positives.
That is the confusion matrix. The columns are the truth. The rows are what the model said.
Sensitivity looks down the sick column. Of everyone who is truly sick, how many did we catch? Ninety out of a hundred. Ninety percent.
Specificity looks down the healthy column. Of everyone who is truly healthy, how many did the model clear? Ninety-five percent.
P P V reads across the alarm row. When the model raises an alarm, how often is the patient really sick? Ninety out of ninety-five. About ninety-five percent.
And N P V reads across the no-alarm row. When the model stays quiet, how often is the patient really healthy? Ninety-five out of a hundred and five. About ninety percent.
Here is the trick to remember. Sensitivity and specificity start from the truth. P P V and N P V start from what the model said.

Which one matters most depends on the cost of each mistake. If missing a sick patient is dangerous, you need high sensitivity. If false alarms waste time and cause worry, look at specificity and P P V.
